column1: phases|Which Node.js event-loop phases matter when comparing timers, I/O, and setImmediate?|Timers run eligible timer callbacks, poll processes I/O, check runs setImmediate, and close callbacks run in a later phase. Promise jobs and nextTick are separate queues, not event-loop phases. Ordering also depends on scheduling context and Node/libuv version.|timer;poll;check;microtask~nextTick|Promise microtasks are an ordinary poll phase.|Explain why a diagram of event-loop phases alone cannot determine every nextTick, Promise, timer, and I/O order.|Account for queue draining after callbacks, module evaluation context, and version. State which callbacks were scheduled from top level versus inside an I/O callback before predicting exact output.|node-loop,node-process|poll

nexttick|What is process.nextTick, and why can recursive use starve I/O?|nextTick callbacks run after the current JavaScript operation before the event loop continues. Repeatedly filling the nextTick queue can prevent I/O progress. In current Node documentation queueMicrotask is generally preferred for portable deferral where appropriate.|current~stack;queue;starv~I/O|nextTick callbacks run in the next timers phase.|A service recursively calls process.nextTick to drain a million work items. Why does the socket stop responding?|The queue can starve the loop. Bound each batch and yield with setImmediate or another suitable scheduling boundary; measure responsiveness and backpressure.|node-process,node-loop|nextTick

promises|How are Promise reactions and queueMicrotask scheduled in JavaScript?|They enqueue microtasks that execute after the current synchronous work at a microtask checkpoint. They do not create worker threads. Jobs queued while draining can extend the checkpoint and starve later tasks if unbounded.|microtask;sync~synchronous;thread~starv|Each Promise callback runs on a new thread.|Predict the CJS output: console.log('A'); Promise.resolve().then(()=>console.log('B')); console.log('C').|The order is A, C, B because the synchronous logs finish before the queued Promise reaction. Specify ordinary CommonJS execution without extra scheduling hooks.|node-process,js-promises|microtask

cjs-esm|Can nextTick and Promise callbacks have different top-level ordering in CJS and ESM?|Yes. In ordinary CJS top-level scheduling nextTick callbacks precede Promise jobs. ESM module evaluation occurs as part of an asynchronous job, so Promise or queueMicrotask jobs can precede a nextTick queued during that evaluation. State the module context.|CommonJS~CJS;ESM~module;context~evaluation|nextTick always runs before every Promise in every module context.|A test asserts nextTick before Promise for an .mjs file and fails. What assumption needs correction?|Do not generalize the CJS top-level example to ESM. Reproduce the exact module and Node version and assert documented ordering only within that context.|node-process|CommonJS

node20-timers|What changed in timer scheduling with libuv 1.45 and Node.js 20?|Starting with libuv 1.45 as used in Node 20, the recurring loop runs timers after poll rather than the earlier pre-poll scheduling. A compatibility timer run can occur before entering the loop. This affects timer/immediate comparisons; it does not guarantee all top-level orders.|1.45~20;after poll;guarantee~context|Node 20 guarantees setTimeout zero always runs before setImmediate.|Does setTimeout(fn,0) versus setImmediate(fn) have one portable top-level order across all Node versions?|No. Specify version and scheduling context. In an I/O callback setImmediate is scheduled for check; top-level timer eligibility and setup timing must not be treated as a universal order.|node-loop|1.45

starvation|How can Promise recursion starve the Node.js event loop without blocking in a while loop?|A chain that continually enqueues microtasks can keep the microtask queue nonempty, delaying timers and I/O. An await of an already resolved promise alone is not necessarily an event-loop yield. Process bounded batches and yield to a later phase.|microtask;timer~I/O;batch~yield|Awaiting Promise.resolve always yields to the next I/O phase.|An async loop awaits Promise.resolve on each iteration yet delays heartbeat timers. Explain and fix it.|The continuation remains in microtasks. Periodically yield with setImmediate or redesign bounded concurrency and batching so other phases can run.|node-process,node-loop|microtask

async-errors|Why does try/catch around an unawaited async call fail to catch its rejection?|An async function returns a Promise. A synchronous try/catch does not handle a later rejection unless the promise is awaited inside it or a catch handler is attached. Propagate meaningful errors and avoid silently swallowing them.|Promise;await~catch;reject|Synchronous try/catch catches every later Promise rejection.|A request handler calls saveAsync() inside try/catch without await and reports success before save fails. Correct it.|Await saveAsync inside the try block or return its promise to a framework that handles rejection. Send success only after the required persistence completes.|node-errors,js-promises|Promise

unhandled|What must be specified before predicting Node behavior for an unhandled rejection?|Node version, --unhandled-rejections mode, and installed process handlers matter. In current default throw behavior an unhandled rejection can become an uncaught exception and terminate the process. Catch at operation boundaries; do not use a global listener as a correctness mechanism.|version~mode;throw~terminate~exception;catch|Unhandled rejections are always harmless warnings on every Node version.|A service stayed up on an old Node release but exits after an upgrade when a background promise rejects. Diagnose it.|Inspect the runtime version and rejection mode, reproduce the missing handler, and attach explicit error handling or supervision. Do not rely on a warning-only historical default.|node-process|unhandledRejection

concurrency|How do Node.js concurrency and parallelism differ?|Concurrency overlaps progress on multiple tasks, such as nonblocking I/O. Parallelism executes work at the same time on different execution resources. One JavaScript event-loop thread does not make every operation single-threaded; workers and native pools can perform parallel work.|overlap~concurr;parallel;worker~pool|Node is incapable of parallel execution.|A CPU-heavy parser blocks all requests despite async route functions. What architecture helps?|Move CPU-bound work to worker threads or a separate process with a bounded pool. Keep request cancellation, queue limits, serialization overhead, and error propagation explicit.|node-worker,node-loop|parallel

workers|When are worker threads useful versus the libuv worker pool?|worker_threads run JavaScript in separate execution contexts and suit CPU-bound JavaScript. Native asynchronous APIs may use libuv workers for operations such as filesystem or crypto. Workers are not usually needed to make ordinary nonblocking network I/O asynchronous.|CPU;JavaScript;libuv~filesystem|Worker threads and the libuv worker pool are the same queue.|A developer creates one worker per HTTP request to wait for fetch. Evaluate this design.|The network operation already supports asynchronous I/O; per-request workers add startup and transfer overhead. Reserve a bounded reusable worker pool for CPU work and benchmark it.|node-worker|CPU

backpressure|What does Writable.write returning false mean in Node streams?|The chunk was accepted but the buffered amount reached the stream's high-water mark. Stop writing until drain before continuing; false is not a rejected-write signal. pipeline coordinates backpressure, completion, and failures across streams.|accepted~buffer;drain;highWaterMark~water mark|Writable.write false means the chunk was discarded.|A producer ignores false from write and a service runs out of memory. How should it be repaired?|Pause production when write returns false, resume after drain, and handle errors or use pipeline. Bound queues and test with a slow destination.|node-stream|drain

retry-policy|Which failures should a Node.js API client retry?|Retry transient failures under a bounded deadline and attempt budget, with exponential backoff and jitter. Respect throttling signals and distinguish terminal validation/authentication failures. Retry side effects only with an idempotency design; a timeout does not prove the server did nothing.|transient;idempot~side effect;budget~deadline;jitter|Every failed POST is safe to retry immediately.|A payment POST times out after the server might have committed. How should the client recover?|Reuse an idempotency key and reconcile the operation status. Do not create a fresh payment on every retry; bound retries and handle ambiguous completion.|aws-retry,aws-idempotency|idempot

circuit-node|What states and transitions does a circuit breaker need?|Closed permits normal attempts, open rejects or degrades without calling the dependency, and half-open permits limited probes after a cooldown. Use a bounded error window and distinguish failure recovery from retries or rate limits.|closed;open;half-open~probe|A circuit breaker retries failed requests forever.|A dependency is failing and every request triggers three retries, worsening load. Where does a breaker help?|Open the circuit when failure thresholds are exceeded, fail fast or degrade, then allow a limited recovery probe. Coordinate retry budgets so each layer does not multiply attempts.|aws-retry|overload

js-const|Does const make a JavaScript object immutable, and can a const accumulator be incremented?|const creates a non-reassignable lexical binding; it does not freeze the referenced object. Mutating an object's properties can be allowed, but reassigning or compound-updating a const numeric binding throws at runtime. Use let for intentional reassignment.|binding;object~propert;let~reassign|Const makes every referenced object deeply immutable.|Spot the issue: function sum(xs){ const total=0; for(const x of xs){total+=x;} return total; }|The compound assignment attempts to reassign total and throws for a nonempty input. Declare total with let; changing the loop variable declaration is not the needed fix.|js-mdn|binding

async-map|Why does async forEach not await all callbacks, and what should replace it?|forEach ignores the promises returned by its callbacks. Use for...of with await for sequential work or map plus Promise.all for bounded appropriate parallel work. Promise.all fails fast but does not automatically cancel already started tasks.|forEach;Promise.all~for...of;cancel~concurr|Awaiting forEach waits for all asynchronous callbacks.|A function does await rows.forEach(async row=>save(row)) then closes the database. Explain the race and fix it.|forEach returns undefined, so the await does not wait for saves. Await a sequential loop or Promise.all of mapped saves, with a concurrency limit and failure policy.|js-promises|Promise.all
